prize_parts.citation: For the development of massively parallel DNA sequencing by synthesis, built on reversible-terminator nucleotide chemistry and clonal single-molecule readout

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: Balasubramanian and Klenerman for sequencing by synthesis. The achievement rests on identifiable chemistry (reversible 3'-blocked fluorescent nucleotides, polymerase incorporation, surface attachment and clonal cluster or single-molecule readout), it has been independently reproduced at enormous scale for two decades, and it changed what researchers and clinicians can do, from population genomics to tumour profiling and pathogen surveillance. The round-1 exchange sharpened rather than weakened the case: Chabes and I now agree on a two-name configuration, and the chair's question about whether a two-name citation on reversible-terminator chemistry is defensible has a direct answer if the citation names the step honoured and not the whole platform field. That is how I would answer Linke's point that the citation must say which step the committee honours.
statement.case_against: Credit remains crowded. Rothberg's pyrosequencing platform was first to market, Mayer's colony sequencing and Ju's terminator chemistry are parallel contributions, and any cut leaves out serious claimants. Somfai, Zou and Aqvist are also right that sequencing can be read as a platform technology in which optics, engineering and commercial competition matter alongside chemistry. I cannot show that the committee will accept the chemistry-versus-technology line as I draw it. I also concede that B058 has the broadest support in the room and that B021 has the cleanest attribution, so my preference rests on a judgement about impact and chemical content, not on a count of support.

responses.point: Somfai argues that sequencing is a platform in which optics, engineering and commercial competition matter, and that a prize crediting one clean chemical advance is safer; he would favour B052 if the committee goes toward biology-facing chemistry.
responses.response: The line is real, but I think it can be drawn inside the citation. The honoured step is the nucleotide chemistry: reversible terminators, linkers and fluorophores that make a polymerase read one base per cycle, which is a molecular design problem of the same kind as a ligand design problem. Optics and instruments enable it, but the Solexa chemistry is what other platforms were later measured against. I do not accept that B021 is the safer choice on that ground alone, but I agree with you that B021 has the cleaner attribution and I keep it as an alternative. On B052 I differ: the single driver is clear, but the timing relative to the 2020 prize persuades me to wait.

responses.point: Zou finds B028 less secure than B021 until a defensible set of names is fixed, and notes that C-N coupling is distinct from the 2010 C-C prize, with thirty years of validation and a clean pair.
responses.response: Your answer on B021 is persuasive on novelty: ligand-controlled C-N coupling needed new catalyst design, not just a new substrate, so I no longer read it as a mere extension of 2010. That moves B021 up in my own ordering and I now list it as my second alternative. Where I still differ is reach: the method mostly changes how chemists work, while sequencing changed what clinicians and population scientists can do. On names, I think the committee can fix a defensible set: the two who conceived and built the reversible-terminator, cluster-readout approach, with the citation worded to say so. I note you would support that core if the committee goes this way.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks B028 sixth because Rothberg, Mayer and Ju each have a parallel claim and wants the chemistry-versus-technology question and priority chronology settled before moving it ahead of base editing and Car-Parrinello.
responses.response: Fair, and I will state the chronology as I understand it rather than leave it vague. Pyrosequencing (454) and Lynx colony sequencing are chemically different routes; the reversible-terminator route is the one that scaled and which a chemical citation can isolate. Ju's terminator chemistry is a contribution to that route, and a three-name cut could not reconcile it with Rothberg and Mayer without arbitrary choices, which is why I prefer to say plainly that the citation honours one lineage. That my account rests on recollection is a limit I acknowledge. I also respect your deaminase argument for B052 but I stay with timing and Kondo and Nishida as my reasons for not preferring it. I do not see Car-Parrinello as competing with B028 and I would not oppose it as a coherent theory prize.

responses.point: Sparr pairs B044 with B058, naming Cullis alone for ionizable lipid nanoparticles, and asks whether anchoring B028 on two names is defensible given Chabes's opening.
responses.response: On B058 we still agree on the science: the pKa-tuned ionizable lipid is the molecular design principle I value most among the biology-facing candidates, which is why it is my first alternative. A Cullis-only part is clean on paper but, as you concede, unfair to Hope and Madden, and the 2023 Medicine prize makes me hesitant. I have not found a three-name allocation I can defend, and the chair's question did not give me one. So I do not move it above B028. On the two-name anchor for B028, Chabes has now dropped Rothberg, so the choice is no longer split inside the sequencing camp. I would not join your two-part configuration because I find a single coherent achievement stronger than a combination of two.

responses.point: Chabes now supports Balasubramanian and Klenerman and warns that, if colleagues think leaving out Rothberg and Ju is unfair, we should say so openly, not hide it behind a vague citation.
responses.response: I agree and I have changed the citation wording accordingly: it now names sequencing by synthesis, reversible-terminator chemistry and clonal readout, not the whole field of massively parallel sequencing. I still hold that I would accept Rothberg only if the committee judges that a prize on the field as a whole needs three names, but that is a fallback, not my position.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards massively parallel sequencing as chemistry rather than biological technology; I judge the enabling steps chemical but not all members do.
Whether a two-name prize can be defended against the claims of Rothberg, Mayer and Ju; my priority account rests on recollection, not verified sources.
Whether the ionizable lipid nanoparticle credit can be allocated in three names and how much weight the 2023 Medicine prize should carry; I could not settle it.
Whether C-N coupling is distinct enough from the 2010 prize; I now lean yes, which makes B021 a stronger fallback than I had judged.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal. Linköping and my postdoc mentors (Stevens, Boey) are not credited on any shortlisted candidate. My scientific overlap with Emma Sparr (peptide-lipid self-assembly) bears on B058 and B044, which I am not preferring, and my nanoparticle-biosensor work gives me familiarity with surface-attachment chemistry relevant to B028 but no tie to any credited name.
